old text: Following the success of assault guns on the World War II Eastern Front, the Hungarians developed their own model, based on the chassis of the Turan tank. There were two designs, the 44M Zrinyi I, incorporated a long 43M 75mm gun, but it did not pass the prototype stage. The 40/43M Zrinyi II was armed with a 40M 105mm L/20 howitzer.The Zrinyi II design was a traditional infantry support vehicle. The Zrinyi I was hoped to fulfill an anti-tank role.Between 40 and 66 Zrinyi II units were produced between August 1943 and July 1944 and a single Zrinyi I prototype. There is only one surviving Zrinyi II in the Kubinka tank museum near Moscow.
new text: The 44M Zrinyi I is a Hungarian assault gun prototype on the Turan chassis, armed with a long 43M 75mm gun. It is meant for the anti-tank role.

old text: The Churchill Kangaroo is the answer to the question of \"What if you had a half-track which you can't destroy?\"
new text: The Churchill Kangaroo carries troops like a half-track but is far harder to destroy.

old text: A carried ammunition crate which supplies heavy ammunition. Supplies British AP, APC, APCBC and HE shells of all calibers. Also contains US 75-76mm AP and HE shells.
new text: A carried ammunition crate which supplies heavy ammunition. Supplies British AP, APC, APCBC and HE shells of all calibers, plus US 75-76mm AP and HE shells.

old text: The Universal Carrier is the best gun platform for transporting troops, eliminating enemy troops and carrying equipment. You can count on them!
new text: The Universal Carrier is a versatile gun platform for transporting troops, carrying equipment and fighting enemy infantry.

old text: The Ordnance ML 3-inch mortar is an British 3-inch (in reality, 81.2 millimeter) calibre mortar. It was a successor to the Stokes mortar and while having an unsatisfactory initial range compared to its German counterparts, the weapon was improved throughout the war and became an effective infantry mortar.
new text: The Ordnance ML 3-inch is a British 81.2 mm infantry mortar, successor to the Stokes mortar. Its early range was poor next to German mortars, but wartime improvements made it effective.

old text: A 3-inch mortar in a Universal Carrier. Isn't this combination... just lovely?^^
new text: A 3-inch mortar mounted in a Universal Carrier.

old text: Mass-produced since April 1943, this self-propelled artillery gun was mainly used for infantry support. The 105mm field howitzer was mounted upon the chassis of a medium M3 tank, reinforcing the armament with a large-calibre AA machine gun. The impressive firepower of the main gun was supplemented by thick armor and excellent manoeuvrability for its class. The only shortcoming of the Priest was its open turret that left the crew vulnerable.
new text: The Priest is a 105mm self-propelled howitzer for infantry support on an M3 medium tank chassis, with a large-calibre AA machine gun. Thick armor protects it, but the open turret exposes the crew.

old text: Before entering World War I, the United States was poorly equipped with heavy artillery. To address this problem a number of foreign heavy artillery guns were adopted, including the Canon de 155 mm GPF. After the end of the war development work began in the United States on a design to improve upon the existing models of heavy gun and carriage. A number of prototypes were produced in the 1920s and 1930s, but the projects were put on hold due to lack of funds. In 1938 the 155 mm Gun T4 on Carriage T2 was finally adopted as 155mm gun M1 on Carriage M1.
new text: The Long Tom, adopted in 1938 as the 155mm gun M1 on Carriage M1, is a US heavy gun developed to replace foreign designs such as the French 155 mm GPF.

old text: In 1940 the British Army concluded that the only heavy howitzer available to it, the First World War-era BL 8-inch howitzer, had insufficient range for the conditions of the Second World War. As a stopgap the decision was made to re-line the existing barrels to a smaller calibre and develop a new range of ammunition to achieve the desired ranges. As expected, this artillery piece has devastating destructive power unrivalled by its contemporaries. Use it wisely and aim well.
new text: This British heavy howitzer is a BL 8-inch howitzer relined to a smaller calibre, with new ammunition for longer range. Its destructive power is unrivalled, so use it wisely and aim well.

old text: One of the most successful German motorcycle models entered mass production in 1934. Fast, and armed with an MG 42 machine-gun (mounted on a sidecar), the R-12 became very popular in suicide missions amongst the Wehrmacht motorized troops.
new text: The R-12 is a fast German sidecar motorcycle armed with an MG 42. Wehrmacht motorized troops favour it for suicide missions.

old text: Production of this light off-road vehicle began in 1940. Thanks to its simplicity and reliability, the Kubelwagen soon became one of the most famous vehicles of World War II, and a symbol of the German Army. Its air-cooled engine worked equally well in hot African conditions and the freezing Russian climate, while its low vehicle weight had a positive effect on its cross-country ability. This model has a mounted MG 42.
new text: The Kubelwagen is a simple, reliable light off-road vehicle with a mounted MG 42. Its air-cooled engine and low weight make it dependable in any climate and good across country.

old text: This half-track was adopted in 1939 for infantry to accompany tanks in the attack. While its armour was sufficent to deflect small-arms fire and shell fragments, heavy machine guns, anti-tank weaponry or any kind of artillery could destroy this half-track with ease.
new text: The SdKfz 250/1 is a half-track that carries infantry alongside attacking tanks. Its armour stops small arms and fragments, but heavy MGs, anti-tank weapons and artillery kill it easily.

old text: This half-track is the bigger brother of the Sd. Kfz. 250. Slightly better armour so sneezing on it will not break the chassis. This model sports a MG 42.
new text: The Sd. Kfz. 251 is the bigger brother of the Sd. Kfz. 250, with slightly better armour and an MG 42.

old text: This half-track is the bigger brother of the Sd. Kfz. 250. Slightly better armour so sneezing on it will not break the chassis. This model sports a MG 34 in the front and a MG 34 in the back for retreating purposes.
new text: The Sd. Kfz. 251 is the bigger brother of the Sd. Kfz. 250, with slightly better armour, an MG 34 in front and a second MG 34 at the rear for covering a retreat.

old text: One of the most successful German motorcycle models entered mass production in 1934. Fast, and armed with an MG 34 machine-gun (mounted on a sidecar), the R-12 became very popular in suicide missions amongst the Wehrmacht motorized troops.
new text: The R-12 is a fast German sidecar motorcycle armed with an MG 34. Wehrmacht motorized troops favour it for suicide missions.

old text: Production of this light off-road vehicle began in 1940. Thanks to its simplicity and reliability, the Kubelwagen soon became one of the most famous vehicles of World War II, and a symbol of the German Army. Its air-cooled engine worked equally well in hot African conditions and the freezing Russian climate, while its low vehicle weight had a positive effect on its cross-country ability. This model has a mounted MG 34.
new text: The Kubelwagen is a simple, reliable light off-road vehicle with a mounted MG 34. Its air-cooled engine and low weight make it dependable in any climate and good across country.

old text: The FlaK 38 was a light anti-aircraft gun used by Germany. It was the most numerous German artillery piece produced during the war. It was used against infantry and light targets with devastating effectiveness, however it lacked the fire rate and the explosive payload to effectively use against aircraft.
new text: The FlaK 38 is Germany's most numerous light anti-aircraft gun and devastating against infantry and light targets. It lacks the fire rate and payload to be effective against aircraft.

old text: This weapon combines four FlaK 38s on a quad mount. While not particularly effective against armoured vehicles, it is an effective weapon against aircraft and soft ground targets. However, due to its rapid fire rate, it consumes ammunition at a rapid pace.
new text: The Flakvierling 38 combines four FlaK 38s on a quad mount, effective against aircraft and soft ground targets but not armour. Its rapid fire uses up ammunition fast.

old text: The 37mm FlaK 36 was the solution to the ever-increasing speeds of fighters and ground-attack aircraft. It fired a payload eight times larger than the 20mm FlaK 38, making it way more effective against high-flying aircraft and armoured targets.
new text: The 37mm FlaK 36 is an anti-aircraft gun firing a payload eight times larger than the 20mm FlaK 38. It is far more effective against high-flying aircraft and armoured targets.

old text: The 150mm sIG 33 was a \"heavy infantry gun\" used by the German army. No one is sure what they were thinking when they classified this 2-ton monstrosity as an infantry gun but nonetheless, its explosive payload can demolish groups of infantry, emplacements and basically destroy any armoured vehicle. Beware of counter-artillery fire and stray Staghounds.
new text: The 150mm sIG 33 is a 2-ton heavy infantry gun whose explosive payload demolishes infantry, emplacements and almost any armoured vehicle. Beware of counter-artillery fire.

old text: In 1942, a variant of the StuG III Ausf. F was designed with a 105 mm (4.1 in) howitzer instead of the 7.5 cm StuK 40 L/43 cannon. These new vehicles, designated StuH 42 (Sturmhaubitze 42, Sd.Kfz 142/2), were designed to provide infantry support with the increased number of StuG III Ausf. F/8 and Ausf. Gs being used in the anti-tank role. The StuH 42 mounts a LeFH 18 howitzer on a StuG III chassis. This vehicle is suitable for both demolishing fortifications, laying down a smoke shield, limited anti-tank work and wasting HEAT on half-tracks. To add to the fun, the vehicle has a sub-standard reload time so using it as a tank destroyer is utterly fruitless and has a very limited range so using it as an artillery piece is not advised either.
new text: The StuH 42 is a StuG III with a 105 mm LeFH 18 howitzer for demolishing fortifications, laying smoke and some anti-tank work. Slow reload and short range suit neither tank hunting nor artillery.

old text: The StuIG 33B answers the question \"What if we strapped an infantry gun on a tank chassis?\". Its explosive power is good against fortifications, enemy tanks, large groups of infantry or practically any target as long as you can keep resupplying it with ammunition.
new text: The StuIG 33B is an infantry gun on a tank chassis. Its explosive power works against fortifications, tanks and large groups of infantry, as long as you keep it supplied with ammunition.

old text: The Sturmpanzer IV (nicknamed Stupa) was a German armoured infantry support gun based on the Panzer IV chassis. It carried a StuH43 gun, a derivative of the sIG 33 for demolition work. It was in all ways an upgrade to the StuIG 33B - even better explosive power, capable of blowing even the heaviest enemy tanks up and a strong, 100mm sloped frontal armour in a fixed superstructure. It can be used in a slight arc, shooting at enemies which can't shoot back at you.
new text: The Sturmpanzer IV (Stupa) carries a StuH43 demolition gun and 100mm sloped frontal armour on a Panzer IV chassis. It can destroy even the heaviest tanks and fire in a slight arc.

old text: The 75mm leIG 18 was an infantry support gun of the Wehrmacht used during World War II. It was used for infantry support and attacking emplacements. It has a mediocre HEAT round used for anti-tank defense.
new text: The 75mm leIG 18 is a Wehrmacht infantry support gun for attacking emplacements. Its HEAT round gives only mediocre anti-tank defense.

old text: The 88mm PaK 43 is an 88mm anti-tank gun developed to penetrate the heaviest of Allied tanks, including the American M26 Pershing, British Churchill Mk. VIII and the Soviet IS-2. A highly effective weapon, it is easily considered one of the best anti-tank weapons our superior German engineers have created so far!
new text: The 88mm PaK 43 is an anti-tank gun built to penetrate the heaviest Allied tanks, including the M26 Pershing, Churchill Mk. VIII and IS-2. It is a highly effective weapon.

old text: The 88mm PaK 44 is a 128mm anti-tank and anti-everything gun conceived from encountering the Russian 122mm cannons. Originally it was supposed to be a field gun but with the encountering of heavy Russian armour its role was expanded to an anti-tank role. Most copies were assembled with stolen French and Russian carriages using superior German engineering. Its weight of 11 tons made it unsuitable for towing so the crew just usually fled upon the enemy approaching.
new text: The PaK 44 is a 128mm anti-tank and field gun built to answer Russian 122mm guns and heavy armour. At 11 tons it is too heavy to tow, so crews usually flee when the enemy approaches.

old text: The 88mm FlaK 36 was an anti-aircraft and anti-tank gun, mounted on a gun carriage that enabled it to fire in all directions. Widespread production started in 1933, and it soon proved to be the best anti-aircraft weapon available when Germany intervened during the Spanish Civil War. It also turned out to be an excellent anti-tank weapon, as its high muzzle velocity and large calibre gave it the power and range to take out enemy armour. The success of this weapon lead to many variants and it was one of the most recognizable German weapons throughout the war. This variant has APCBC, HE, APCR and HEAT ammo available.
new text: The 88mm FlaK 36 is an all-round anti-aircraft gun whose high muzzle velocity and large calibre also make it an excellent long-range anti-tank gun. It has APCBC, HE, APCR and HEAT ammo.

old text: The design of this 81mm gun closely follows its Soviet counterpart, consisting of three main sections: the firing tube, support plate and a two-legged mount. It fires 3.5kg HE rounds via indirect trajectory. Firing is triggered by the pin inside the tube striking the primer of a descending shell.
new text: The sGrW 34 is an 81mm mortar of firing tube, support plate and two-legged mount that fires 3.5kg HE rounds on an indirect trajectory.

old text: This 120mm mortar is a copy of the Soviet PM 38 mortar which is itself a copy of the French 120mm Brandt mortar. Use this totally original design of a mortar to rain down fire on your opponents indiscriminately.
new text: The 120mm sGrW 42 is a copy of the Soviet PM 38 mortar, itself a copy of the French 120mm Brandt mortar. Use it to rain down fire on your opponents.

old text: The SdKfz 250 was a light armoured halftrack very similar in appearance to the larger Hanomag-designed SdKfz 251 which was built by the DEMAG firm for use by Nazi Germany in World War II. SdKfz 250/7 - light armoured halftrack with 81mm GrW 34 mortar.
new text: The SdKfz 250/7 is a light armoured halftrack carrying an 81mm GrW 34 mortar.

old text: The Grille was a series of self propelled artillery vehicles used by Nazi Germany during World War II. The Grille series was based on the Czech Panzer 38(t) tank chassis and used a 150mm sIG 33 infantry gun.
new text: The Grille is a self-propelled artillery vehicle carrying a 150mm sIG 33 infantry gun on the Czech Panzer 38(t) chassis.

old text: The 150mm Nebelwerfer 41 was a German multiple rocket launcher used in the Second World War for saturating fire. Its main drawbacks included heavy smoke generated by the launchers which meant that it had to be relocated quickly due to counter-artillery.
new text: The 150mm Nebelwerfer 41 is a German multiple rocket launcher for saturating fire. Its heavy launch smoke means it must relocate quickly to escape counter-artillery.

old text: The SdKfz 251 \"Stuka Zu Fuss\" was a German World War II multiple rocket launcher. Itwas equipped with the Wurfrahmen 40 (launch frame 40) launcher. (also known as a \"glorified wooden box\") It combined a vehicle such as the SdKfz 251 halftrack with rocket artillery to form a more mobile and protected artillery piece than the towed Nebelwerfer. It was nicknamed Stuka zu Fuss. (Stuka on foot)
new text: The SdKfz 251 Stuka zu Fuss is a half-track with a Wurfrahmen 40 rocket launch frame. It is more mobile and better protected than the towed Nebelwerfer.

old text: The 88mm FlaK 18 was an anti-aircraft and anti-tank gun, mounted on a gun carriage that enabled it to fire in all directions. Widespread production started in 1933, and it soon proved to be the best anti-aircraft weapon available when Germany intervened during the Spanish Civil War. It also turned out to be an excellent anti-tank weapon, as its high muzzle velocity and large calibre gave it the power and range to take out enemy armour. The success of this weapon lead to many variants and it was one of the most recognizable German weapons throughout the war. This variant has APCBC and HE ammo available.
new text: The 88mm FlaK 18 is an all-round anti-aircraft gun whose high muzzle velocity and large calibre also make it an excellent long-range anti-tank gun. It has APCBC and HE ammo.

old text: The 210mm Morser 18 was a German heavy howitzer used in the Second World War by independent artillery battalions and batteries. It was one of the first weapons, if not the first in quantity production, that used the interesting dual-recoil system. If (and that's a big if) its shell hits its intended target, nothing survives in the path of its shockwave.
new text: The 210mm Morser 18 is a German heavy howitzer with a dual-recoil system. If, and it is a big if, its shell hits the target, nothing in the path of its shockwave survives.

old text: The SdKfz 250 was a light armoured halftrack built by the DEMAG firm, for use by Nazi Germany in World War II. The SdKfz 250/10 (37mm PaK) was the reconnaissance platoon leader's variant with 37mm PaK 35/36. This was the same anti-tank gun used in a towed carriage early in the war. It was normally used without the protective shield to conceal the firepower of this gun and look more like a SdKfz 250/1.
new text: The SdKfz 250/10 is the reconnaissance platoon leader's light armoured halftrack with a 37mm PaK 35/36. Usually fitted without a shield, it looks much like a plain SdKfz 250/1.

old text: The SdKfz 250 was a light armoured halftrack very similar in appearance to the larger Hanomag-designed SdKfz 251 which was built by the DEMAG firm for use by Nazi Germany in World War II. SdKfz 250/9 - light armoured halftrack with 20mm KwK 30 gun.
new text: The SdKfz 250/9 is a light armoured halftrack armed with a 20mm KwK 30 gun.

old text: The SdKfz 251 (Sonderkraftfahrzeug 251) half-track was an armored fighting vehicle designed and first built by Nazi Germany's Hanomag company during World War II. They were produced throughout the war. This version was fitted with a 75 mm KwK 37 infantry support gun using the same pedestal gun mount employed on the StuG III. Nicknamed \"Stummel\" (\"stump\").
new text: The SdKfz 251/9 Stummel is a Hanomag half-track armed with a 75 mm KwK 37 infantry support gun on the StuG III pedestal mount.

old text: The SdKfz 234 was an eight-wheeled armoured car used by the German Army in the Second World War. 234/1 - 1 x 20mm KwK 30 L/55 autocannon, 1 x MG 34 Machinegun. This design featured an open-topped turret. Around 200 were produced.
new text: The SdKfz 234/1 is an eight-wheeled armoured car with a 20mm KwK 30 L/55 autocannon and an MG 34 in an open-topped turret.

old text: The SdKfz 234 was an eight-wheeled armoured car used by the German Army in the Second World War. 234/3 - 1 x 75mm K51 L/24 in open-topped superstructure replacing the turret. 88 built between June and December.
new text: The SdKfz 234/3 is an eight-wheeled armoured car with a 75mm K51 L/24 gun in an open-topped superstructure instead of a turret.

old text: The production of the Wehrmacht's last light tank began in 1942. The Lynx, with its 20mm autogun and light armor, did not pose a serious threat to enemy tanks, although its six-gear transmission allowed it to reach high speeds. Thanks to this advantage, it was ideally suited for reconnaissance missions which earned it deserved respect.
new text: The Lynx is the Wehrmacht's last light tank, with a 20mm autogun and light armor. It poses little threat to tanks, but its high speed makes it ideal for reconnaissance.

old text: The PzKpfw IV's turret was removed and replaced with an open-top, hexagonal turret which housed a 37mm FlaK 43. In addition to its intended role as an anti-aircraft weapon, the fast-firing gun was highly effective against light vehicles and minor fortifications. A closed-top design would have been preferable, but this was not possible due to the heavy smoke generated by the gun.
new text: The Ostwind is a PzKpfw IV with an open-top turret housing a 37mm FlaK 43. Besides anti-aircraft work, its fast-firing gun is deadly to light vehicles and minor fortifications.

old text: The SdKfz 251 (Sonderkraftfahrzeug 251) half-track was an armored fighting vehicle designed and first built by Nazi Germany's Hanomag company during World War II. They were produced throughout the war. This version was fitted with a 20mm FlaK 38 anti-aircraft gun. Compared to the 20mm KwK 30, this gun has almost twice the cycling rate.
new text: The SdKfz 251/17 is a Hanomag half-track armed with a 20mm FlaK 38 anti-aircraft gun, which fires almost twice as fast as the 20mm KwK 30.

old text: The Pz.Kpfw. III Ausf. M was a German medium tank. The Panzer III M is armed with a 5 cm high-velocity anti-tank gun. The tank has 50 mm of armour at the front of the hull and 57 on the turret front, but there is an additional 20mm plate on the upper hull and at the front of the turret. Side armour of the hull and turret are 30 mm and are protected by an extra 5 mm plate that protects from HEAT and HE rounds.
new text: The Panzer III Ausf. M is a German medium tank with a 5 cm high-velocity anti-tank gun. Its 50-57 mm front armour carries extra 20 mm plates, and 5 mm side plates guard against HEAT and HE.

old text: In mid-1943 came the last version, the Ausf. N with a short-barrel 75mm KwK 37 L/24 gun capable of firing, for the first time, HEAT projectiles. This tank was the perfect dual-purpose, versatile model, which inspired retrofitting of earlier versions. Since new specialized tank-hunters and heavy battle tanks were available, the Panzer III was increasingly confined to an infantry support role.
new text: The Panzer III Ausf. N is the last Panzer III version, with a short 75mm KwK 37 L/24 gun that fires HEAT rounds. A versatile dual-purpose tank, it mostly serves in infantry support.

old text: The Panther Ausf. G was created as a response to the Soviet T-34 and entered mass production in March 1944. Its relatively good manoeuvrability and a long-barrelled 75mm gun made this tank a dangerous adversary. Its insufficient side protection was compensated for by its excellent frontal armor.
new text: The Panther Ausf. G, a response to the Soviet T-34, combines good manoeuvrability with a long-barrelled 75mm gun. Its excellent frontal armor makes up for weak side protection.

old text: This unit entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1944. Its turret-mounted 88mm long-barrelled gun was capable of destroying any enemy tank from a long distance. Combined with excellent armor, this made the King Tiger the most powerful tank of WWII. The Panzer VI Ausf. B was almost invulnerable to enemy guns, but its-70 ton weight had a negative impact on its mobility.
new text: The King Tiger (Panzer VI Ausf. B) has a long-barrelled 88mm gun that destroys any enemy tank at long range and armor almost no gun can pierce. Its 70-ton weight hurts its mobility.

old text: This unit entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1944. Its turret-mounted 88mm long-barrelled gun was capable of destroying any enemy tank from a long distance. Combined with excellent armor, this made the King Tiger the most powerful tank of WWII. The Panzer VI Ausf. B was almost invulnerable to enemy guns, but its 70-ton weight had a negative impact on its mobility.
new text: The King Tiger (Panzer VI Ausf. B) has a long-barrelled 88mm gun that destroys any enemy tank at long range and armor almost no gun can pierce. Its 70-ton weight hurts its mobility.

old text: In April 1943, another modification of the most popular German tank came to the front. This machine differed from its predecessors, having enhanced armor and improved armament. Its armor was 80mm thick, and the mounted screens on its sides ensured reliable protection from high-explosion rounds. The new long-barrelled KwK 40 L/48 boasted excellent combat performance and was successfully used to fight medium enemy tanks.
new text: The Panzer IV Ausf. H has 80mm armor, side screens against high-explosive rounds and a long-barrelled KwK 40 L/48 gun. It fights enemy medium tanks well.

old text: The Panzer IV Ausf. J was a cost-cutting measure in order to produce more Panzer IVs. This variant had its electric turret drive removed which meant that the turret had to be hand-cranked. It was replaced by an additional fuel tank and the number of return rollers was reduced from 4 to 3.
new text: The Panzer IV Ausf. J is a cost-cutting Panzer IV with a hand-cranked turret, its electric turret drive replaced by an extra fuel tank.

old text: The Panther Ausf. D was created as a response to the Soviet T-34 and entered mass production in January 1943. Its relatively good manoeuvrability and a long-barrelled 75mm gun made this tank a dangerous adversary. Its insufficient side protection was compensated for by its excellent frontal armor.
new text: The Panther Ausf. D, a response to the Soviet T-34, combines good manoeuvrability with a long-barrelled 75mm gun. Its excellent frontal armor makes up for weak side protection.

old text: SdKfz 234/4 'Pakwagen' - 1 x 75mm PaK 40 L/46 in open-topped superstructure replacing the turret. 89 built between December 1944 and March 1945. The design was really overloaded but fairly effective.
new text: The SdKfz 234/4 Pakwagen carries a 75mm PaK 40 L/46 in an open-topped superstructure instead of a turret. Badly overloaded, it is still fairly effective.

old text: The Jagdpanzer IV, SdKfz 162, was a German tank destroyer based on the Panzer IV chassis with 7.5 cm Pak 39 L/48. 769-784 tank destroyers have been produced in January 1944 - November 1944.
new text: The Jagdpanzer IV is a German tank destroyer on the Panzer IV chassis, armed with a 7.5 cm Pak 39 L/48.

old text: The StuG III assault gun, mounted on the PzKpfw III chassis, entered production in March 1942 and was mainly used as a means of defense from enemy counter-attacks. Its low profile and sturdy, sloping frontal armor helped increase its overall resilience which, combined with its turret-mounted 75mm gun, allowed the tank to accomplish combat objectives with maximum efficiency. Anti-HEAT armor plates were frequently mounted on the sides to further improve its defensive capabilities.
new text: The StuG III Ausf. G is a low-profile assault gun with a 75mm gun, used mainly against enemy counter-attacks. Sloped frontal armor and anti-HEAT side plates make it hard to kill.

old text: StuG III Ausf. F/8 September-December 1942, 250 produced. Introduction of an improved hull design similar to that used for the Panzer III Ausf. J / L with increased rear armour. From October 1942, 30 mm thick plates of additional armour were bolted on to speed up the production line. From F/8, the 75mm StuK 40 L/48 gun was standard until the very last of the Ausf. G. Due to the lack of double baffle muzzle brakes, a few L/48 guns mounted on F/8s were fitted with the single baffle ball type muzzle brake found in Panzer IV Ausf. F2/G.
new text: The StuG III Ausf. F/8 has an improved hull with thicker rear armour, bolted-on 30 mm extra plates and the 75mm StuK 40 L/48 gun.

old text: One of the most successful German motorcycle models entered mass production in 1934. Fast, and armed with an MG-34 machine-gun (mounted on a sidecar), the R-12 became very popular amongst the Wehrmacht motorized troops.
new text: The R-12 is a fast German sidecar motorcycle armed with an MG-34, popular with Wehrmacht motorized troops.

old text: The Kfz.15 Horch Were supplied to the Wehrmacht between 1936 and 1943 in the three versions Leichter Einheits-PKW, Mittlerer Einheits-PKW and Schwerer Einheits-PKW (light, medium and heavy passenger car). These vehicles were supposed to replace the civilian vehicles previously procured by the Reichswehr with cross-country mobile vehicles that conformed with military requirements while simplifying logistics and maintenance by using standardized components. The program achieved neither of these goals.
new text: The Kfz.15 Horch is a cross-country Wehrmacht passenger car built from 1936 to 1943. It was meant to simplify logistics with standardized parts, but never did.

old text: Supply trucks carrying fuel canisters, repair kits, ammunition, grenades and other equipment.\nThe Opel Blitz, a reliable and easily maintained vehicle, was present in all theatres of WWII. It was ideally suited for harsh battlefield conditions and was modified to serve a variety of functions, from ambulance truck to mobile HQ. The Blitz is perfect for transporting troops and towing artillery.
new text: The Opel Blitz supply truck carries fuel canisters, repair kits, ammunition, grenades and other equipment. Reliable and easy to maintain, it also transports troops and tows artillery.

old text: Supply trucks carrying crates of armor-piercing and high-explosive rounds, as well as repair kits.\nThe Opel Blitz, a reliable and easily maintained vehicle, was present in all theatres of WWII. It was ideally suited for harsh battlefield conditions and was modified to serve a variety of functions, from ambulance truck to mobile HQ. The Blitz is perfect for transporting troops and towing artillery.
new text: The Opel Blitz supply truck carries crates of armor-piercing and high-explosive rounds and repair kits. Reliable and easy to maintain, it also transports troops and tows artillery.

old text: Inside this truck you will find tools for repairing equipment, materials for building obstacles and defenses, and anti-personnel and anti-tank mines. Obstacles are usually built in front of occupied positions or occasionally on the flanks and in the gaps between them. defenses are made of sandbags and serve to strengthen the positions of friendly infantry.\nThe Opel Blitz, a reliable and easily maintained vehicle, was present in all theatres of WWII. It was ideally suited for harsh battlefield conditions and was modified to serve a variety of functions, from ambulance truck to mobile HQ. Suitable for the fast redeployment of troops on a massive scale and for towing artillery.
new text: The Opel Blitz engineer truck carries repair tools, materials for obstacles and sandbag defenses, and anti-personnel and anti-tank mines. It can also redeploy troops fast and tow artillery.

old text: The PaK 36 being a small-calibre weapon, it was found to be inadequate against allied medium and heavy tanks. Still, the gun was effective against the most common light tanks. During the initial phases of Operation Barbarossa the PaK 36 could still penetrate the majority of Soviet tanks at ranges up to 1000m from the front.
new text: The PaK 36 is a small-calibre anti-tank gun, effective against the most common light tanks but inadequate against Allied medium and heavy tanks.

old text: The 50mm PaK 38 was the successor to the 37mm PaK 36, and the predecessor to the 75mm PaK 40. When the Soviets introduced their T-34, the PaK 38 was one of the few anti-tank guns capable of penetrating its armor at the time. Though this weapon was replaced by the PaK 40 and other more-powerful anti-tank weapons, the PaK 38 remained in useful service until the end of the war.
new text: The 50mm PaK 38 is the successor to the 37mm PaK 36 and one of the few early guns able to penetrate the T-34. Though replaced by the PaK 40, it stays useful to the end of the war.

old text: The first guns of this type appeared during the spring of 1942, on the Eastern Front. The PaK 40 was designed to take on tanks and armored vehicles, however, its fairly large calibre and the availability of high-explosive rounds allowed it to be used to suppress weapon emplacements, demolish light fortifications and eliminate enemy personnel. Its accuracy and effective range exceed that of the Soviet ZIS-3 field artillery gun.
new text: The PaK 40 is an anti-tank gun whose large calibre and HE rounds also let it hit emplacements, light fortifications and infantry. Its accuracy and range exceed the Soviet ZIS-3.

old text: The le. FH 18 was the standard field howitzer used by the Wehrmacht during World War II, capable of firing a 15kg projectile a distance of nearly 11 kilometres, at a rate of about 5 rounds per minute. During the war it underwent several modifications to increase various areas of performance, and it remained in active use throughout the entire war.
new text: The le. FH 18 is the Wehrmacht's standard field howitzer, firing a 15kg projectile nearly 11 kilometres at about 5 rounds per minute.

old text: The Wespe married the Panzer II tank chassis (which was no longer viable as a tank after 1940), to the 105 mm leFH 18 Howitzer, producing a self-propelled artillery unit which proved both functional and reliable. This combination afforded it a place in armored artillery battalions, serving alongside the heavier Hummel self-propelled guns. It proved to be a very successful vehicle when it first saw combat on the Eastern Front, and soon all Panzer II production was dedicated to turning out these vehicles. Nearly 700 had been produced by the end of the war.
new text: The Wespe is a reliable self-propelled artillery unit mounting the 105 mm leFH 18 howitzer on a Panzer II chassis. It serves alongside the heavier Hummel in armored artillery battalions.

old text: The SdKfz 138/1 Was a series of self propelled artillery vehicles used by Nazi Germany during World War II. The Grille series was based on the Czech Panzer 38(t) tank chassis and used a 15 cm sIG 33 infantry gun.
new text: The SdKfz 138/1 Grille is a self-propelled artillery vehicle carrying a 15 cm sIG 33 infantry gun on the Czech Panzer 38(t) chassis.

old text: The SdKfz 251/1 Was a World War II German armored fighting vehicle designed by the Hanomag company, based on its earlier, unarmored SdKfz 11 vehicle. The 251/1 was designed with Rocket launcher called the Stuka zu Fuss equipped with six side mounted frames for launching 280mm or 320mm Wurfkoerper rockets.
new text: The SdKfz 251/1 Stuka zu Fuss is a Hanomag armored half-track with six side-mounted frames for launching 280mm or 320mm Wurfkoerper rockets.

old text: Thanks to its six-cylinder Maybach engine, the Pz.I light tank -- mass produced since July 1943 -- was fast and manoeuvrable, while its turret-mounted double machine guns proved to be excellent against enemy infantry. However, its light armor and lack of sufficient armament rendered the Pz.I useless in tank battles.
new text: The Pz.I is a fast, manoeuvrable light tank whose twin turret machine guns are excellent against infantry. Its light armor and weak armament make it useless in tank battles.

old text: The Flakpanzer I is a self propelled anti-aircraft gun based on the Panzer I chassis. Up to this point, motorized flak vehicles had been unarmored, and prone to small arms fire and other common weapons. Joining a Flak 38 to the readily available Panzer I chassis provided a minimal amount of protection, and the vehicle also had substantial anti-aircraft and anti-infantry capabilities due to its 20mm cannon. However, it still lacked sufficient protection for combat use and crews suffered high casualty rates.
new text: The Flakpanzer I mounts a 20mm Flak 38 on the Panzer I chassis, strong against aircraft and infantry. Its protection is minimal and crews suffer high casualties.

old text: The SdKfz 234 was an eight-wheeled armoured car used by the German Army in the Second World War. 234/1 - 1 x 2 cm KwK 30 L/55 autocannon, 1 x MG34 Machinegun. This design featured an open-topped turret. Around 200 were produced.
new text: The SdKfz 234/1 is an eight-wheeled armoured car with a 2 cm KwK 30 L/55 autocannon and an MG34 in an open-topped turret.

old text: The SdKfz 234 armored, all-wheel drive vehicle was mass produced in 1943. Thanks to sloping armor plates, the hull protected the crew not only from shell fragments and infantry weapons, but also from low-calibre artillery fire. Moreover, the powerful engine allowed the vehicle to achieve high speeds, and its armament proved to be very effective against enemy infantry and lightly-armored vehicles, winning the \"Puma\" the rightfully deserved title of 'best armored car of WWII'.
new text: The SdKfz 234 Puma is a fast armored car whose sloped armor stops fragments, infantry weapons and low-calibre artillery. Its armament is deadly to infantry and light vehicles.

old text: The PzKpfw IV's turret was removed and replaced with an open-top, hexagonal turret which housed a 3.7 cm FlaK 43. In addition to its intended role as an anti-aircraft weapon, the fast-firing gun was highly effective against light vehicles and minor fortifications. A closed-top design would have been preferable, but this was not possible due to the heavy smoke generated by the gun.
new text: The Ostwind is a PzKpfw IV with an open-top turret housing a 3.7 cm FlaK 43. Besides anti-aircraft work, its fast-firing gun is deadly to light vehicles and minor fortifications.

old text: The PzKpfw III entered mass production in September 1939. One year later, it received improved armor, as well as a new, long-barrelled 50mm gun. The tank was able to successfully engage and destroy armored cars and light tanks, although with the appearance of the T-34 it became largely obsolete.
new text: The PzKpfw III, with improved armor and a long-barrelled 50mm gun, can destroy armored cars and light tanks. Against the T-34 it is largely obsolete.

old text: Production of these unsophisticated and cheaply produced tank destroyers started in March 1944 and continued until the end of the war. The 75mm AT gun PaK 39 was mounted on the chassis of a Czech Lt38 light tank, giving the vehicle good mobility. Its compact dimensions, low profile and sloped frontal armor resulted in increased shell resistance but, at the same time, had a negative impact on the amount of ordnance it carried. Despite its insufficient side protection, the Hetzer is widely considered to be one of the most successful vehicles in its class.
new text: The Hetzer is a cheap, mobile tank destroyer with a 75mm PaK 39 on a Czech Lt38 chassis. Its low, sloped front resists shells, but its sides are weak and it carries little ammo.

old text: Mass production of the Nashorn tank destroyer started in February 1943 and continued until the end of the war. Its 88mm gun was merciless towards enemy tanks who had little defense against it. That, combined with its great mobility, made the \"Rhinoceros\" a fearsome weapon. Its frontal armor was thick enough, but the open fighting compartment and almost vertical side armor plates did not provide sufficient protection to the crew.
new text: The Nashorn is a mobile tank destroyer whose 88mm gun is merciless against tanks. Its frontal armor is adequate, but the open fighting compartment and near-vertical sides expose the crew.

old text: The Elefant tank destroyer entered service with the Wehrmacht in the spring of 1943. Its cabin-mounted 88mm gun was considered to be the deadliest weapon of its time, and gave it the capacity to destroy most enemy tanks from beyond their range of effective fire. Its armor -- up to 200mm thick -- made the Elefant impervious to frontal attacks, but its resulting heavy weight limited its speed and hindered its cross-country capability.
new text: The Elefant is a tank destroyer with an 88mm gun that outranges most tanks and up to 200mm of armor, impervious from the front. Its heavy weight makes it slow.

old text: This unit entered service with the German army in 1942 and was considered the best tank right up until the end of 1943. Soviet 45mm guns could not penetrate the Tiger's armor, even at point-blank range, while its 88mm gun was able to destroy any tank of that time.
new text: The Tiger carries an 88mm gun able to destroy any tank of its time, and armor that Soviet 45mm guns cannot pierce even at point-blank range.

old text: The Ausf. G Panther version was created as a response to the Soviet T34, and entered mass production in March 1944. Its relatively good manoeuvrability and a long-barrelled 75mm gun made this tank a dangerous adversary. Its insufficient side protection was compensated for by its excellent frontal armor.
new text: The Panther Ausf. G, a response to the Soviet T34, combines good manoeuvrability with a long-barrelled 75mm gun. Its excellent frontal armor makes up for weak side protection.

old text: This unit entered service with the Wehrmacht in 1944. Its turret-mounted 88mm long-barrelled gun was capable of destroying any enemy tank from a long distance. Combined with excellent armor, this made the King Tiger the most powerful tank of WWII. The Pz VI Ausf.B was almost invulnerable to enemy guns, but its 70 ton weight had a negative impact on its mobility.
new text: The King Tiger (Pz VI Ausf. B) has a long-barrelled 88mm gun that destroys any enemy tank at long range and armor almost no gun can pierce. Its 70-ton weight hurts its mobility.

old text: The Schwimmwagen was a four-wheel drive amphibious vehicle used by the German army in World War II. As opposed to other cars and half-tracks, this one does not catch fire upon contacting water. Upon engine failure paddles can be used as an emergency measure.
new text: The Schwimmwagen is a four-wheel-drive amphibious car that, unlike other cars and half-tracks, does not catch fire in water. Paddles serve as a backup if the engine fails.

old text: The first guns of this type appeared during the spring of 1942, on the Eastern Front. The PaK 40 was designed to take on tanks and armored vehicles, however, its fairly large calibre and the availability of high-explosive rounds allowed it to be used to suppress weapon emplacements, demolish light fortifications and eliminate enemy personnel. Its accuracy and effective range exceed that of the Soviet ZIS-3 field artillery gun.
new text: The PaK 40 is an anti-tank gun whose large calibre and HE rounds also let it hit emplacements, light fortifications and infantry. Its accuracy and range exceed the Soviet ZIS-3.

old text: The SdKfz 251 half-track was an armored fighting vehicle designed and first built by Nazi Germany's Hanomag company during World War II. They were produced throughout the war. This version was fitted with a 37mm PaK 35/36 anti-tank gun.
new text: The SdKfz 251/10 is a Hanomag half-track armed with a 37mm PaK 35/36 anti-tank gun.

old text: The first version of the Panzer IV assault tank turned out to be ineffective against Soviet T34s and KVs. However, by the spring of 1942, the Wehrmacht started receiving new versions of the PzKpfw IV tanks, complete with upgraded armament and long-barrelled anti-tank KwK 40 guns, capable of defeating almost any opponent. In addition, the tank had good manoeuvrability, which -- along with its strong armor and powerful gun -- turned it into a fearsome combat vehicle.
new text: The Panzer IV Ausf. G has a long-barrelled KwK 40 anti-tank gun able to defeat almost any opponent. Good manoeuvrability and strong armor make it a fearsome combat vehicle.

old text: In August 1943, after repairs and modifications to the gearbox and other systems, a new variant of Panther was produced - the Ausf. A, which soon became a formidable weapon. The Panther Ausf. A was the most numerous variant during the Normandy campaign in the summer of 194, and some 400 Panthers of all types were lost there. It featured a redesigned turret, the new cast commander's cupola, a mounting bracket for an anti-aircraft MG 34 on the cupola, a ball-mounted MG 34 in the frontal plate and standard side armor skirts. The side skirts and the brackets holding them had to be removed for transport by rail as the width of the Panther reached the maximum clearance for transport by rail. Over time, five different types of exhaust arrangement were used. In general, from August 1943 to May 1944, some 2,200 were produced by MAN, Daimler-Benz, Demag and Henschel.
new text: The Panther Ausf. A has a redesigned turret, a cast commander's cupola with an anti-aircraft MG 34, a ball-mounted MG 34 in the front plate and side armor skirts.

old text: Tiger I is the common name of a German heavy tank developed in 1942 and used in World War II. It was an answer to the unexpectedly impressive Soviet armour encountered in the initial months of the Axis invasion of the Soviet Union, particularly the T-34 and the KV-1. The Tiger I design gave the Wehrmacht its first tank mounting the 88 mm gun in its initial armored fighting vehicle-dedicated version which in its FlaK version had previously demonstrated its effectiveness against both air and ground targets. During the course of the war, the Tiger I saw combat on all German battlefronts. The initial official German designation was Panzerkampfwagen VI Ausfuhrung H ('Panzer VI version H', abbreviated PzKpfw VI Ausf. H), but the tank was redesignated as PzKpfw VI Ausf. E in March 1943.
new text: The Tiger I is a German heavy tank with an 88 mm gun, built to answer Soviet armour such as the T-34 and KV-1.

old text: The Flammpanzer 38(t) was a Jagdpanzer 38(t) fitted with a Koebe flamethrower. It was perfect for providing Lebensraum (living space) for Germanic Aryan girls.
new text: The Flammpanzer 38(t) is a Jagdpanzer 38(t) fitted with a Koebe flamethrower.

old text: StuG III Ausf. F: (Sd.Kfz 142/1; March-September 1942, 366 produced) The first real up-gunning of the StuG, this version uses the longer 75mm StuK 40 L/43 gun. Firing armor-piercing StuK 40 L/43 could penetrate 91 mm of armor inclined 30 degrees from vertical at 500m, 82mm at 1,000m, 72mm at 1,500m, 63mm at 2,000 m, allowing the Ausf. F to engage most Soviet armored vehicles at normal combat ranges. This change marked the StuG as being more of a tank destroyer than an infantry support vehicle.
new text: The StuG III Ausf. F carries the longer 75mm StuK 40 L/43, which pierces 91 mm of sloped armor at 500m. It can fight most Soviet armored vehicles, more tank destroyer than infantry support.

old text: The Sturmgeschutz IV (StuG IV) (SdKfz 167), was a German assault gun of the Second World War, which also functioned as a tank destroyer in late-war engagements.
new text: The Sturmgeschutz IV (StuG IV, SdKfz 167) is a German assault gun that also serves as a tank destroyer.

old text: The first Type 97 Chi-Ha tanks were armed with the 57mm -- a relic from its predecessor, the Type 89. While this tank improved upon many of the previous Imperial Japanese Army armored concepts, it was still insufficient to take on the Allied tanks of that period. The short-barrelled 57mm gun was well suited for eliminating soft enemy targets, but was ineffective against enemy armor. Relegated to a role of infantry support, the task of engaging enemy armor was left to the later Chi-Ha's, which would sport the 47mm cannon with its longer barrel and increased anti-armor capabilities.
new text: The early Type 97 Chi-Ha has a short-barrelled 57mm gun, good against soft targets but ineffective against armor. It serves in infantry support, leaving tanks to the later 47mm Chi-Ha.

old text: The BA-11 is a heavily-armored vehicle, mass produced since 1938, and used largely as a mobile platform for providing fire support for advancing infantry. Compared to other light tanks, it boasted thicker armor, as well as a greater manoeuvrability and firepower. An upgraded ZIS-16 engine allowed it to reach high speeds, while its turret-mounted 45mm gun gave it the capacity to penetrate the armor of almost all of its contemporary light and medium tanks.
new text: The BA-11 is a fast, heavily armored vehicle for infantry fire support with a turret-mounted 45mm gun. The gun can penetrate almost all light and medium tanks of its time.

old text: The 150mm Nebelwerfer 41 was a German multiple rocket launcher used in the Second World War for saturating fire. Its main drawbacks included heavy smoke generated by the launchers which meant that it had to be relocated quickly due to counter-artillery.
new text: The 150mm Nebelwerfer 41 is a German multiple rocket launcher for saturating fire. Its heavy launch smoke means it must relocate quickly to escape counter-artillery.

old text: The SdKfz 250/1 Was a light armoured halftrack, very similar in appearance to the larger Hanomag-designed SdKfz 251, and built by the DEMAG firm, for use by Nazi Germany in World War II. Most variants were open-topped and had a single access door in the rear mount with a machine gun.
new text: The SdKfz 250/1 is a light armoured halftrack built by DEMAG, similar to the larger SdKfz 251. It is open-topped, with a rear access door and a machine gun.

old text: The Maschinengewehr 34, or MG 34, is a German recoil-operated air-cooled machine gun, first tested in 1929, introduced in 1934, and issued to units in 1936. It introduced an entirely new concept in automatic firepower, the Einheitsmaschinengewehr Universal machine gun and is generally considered the world's first general purpose machine gun.
new text: The MG 34 is a German recoil-operated, air-cooled machine gun, generally considered the world's first general purpose machine gun.

old text: This modification entered service with the Red Army on January 23rd, 1944. In order to mount a powerful 85mm anti-tank gun, some changes had to be introduced into its turret design: it became larger and more heavily protected. Its side and rear armor was also enhanced, which, in combination with its sharp slope angle, significantly increased the shell resistance of the hull. As a result the T-34's weight increased to 32 tons, making the tank a bit slower, but its combat efficiency rose significantly.
new text: This T-34 model has a powerful 85mm anti-tank gun in a larger, better protected turret and stronger side and rear armor. At 32 tons it is a bit slower, but far more effective.

old text: The design of this 81mm gun closely follows its Soviet counterpart, consisting of three main sections: the firing tube, support plate and a two-legged mount. It fires 3.5kg HE rounds via indirect trajectory. Firing is triggered by the pin inside the tube striking the primer of a descending shell.
new text: An 81mm mortar of firing tube, support plate and two-legged mount that fires 3.5kg HE rounds on an indirect trajectory.

old text: In production since 1918, the SFH-18 heavy field howitzer was used by the Wehrmacht troops during WWII, against enemy artillery and personnel, as well as fortifications and trench lines. It fired 43kg HE rounds, capable of dealing devastating damage at very long distances, but the gun's heavy weight impaired its mobility.
new text: The SFH-18 is a heavy field howitzer firing 43kg HE rounds at very long range against artillery, personnel, fortifications and trench lines. Its heavy weight limits its mobility.

old text: In April 1943, another modification of the most popular German tank came to the front. This machine differed from its predecessors, having enhanced armor and improved armament. Its armor was 80mm thick, and the mounted screens on its sides ensured reliable protection from high-explosion rounds. The new long-barrelled Kwk40 L/48 boasted excellent combat performance and was successfully used to fight medium enemy tanks.
new text: The Panzer IV Ausf. H has 80mm armor, side screens against high-explosive rounds and a long-barrelled Kwk40 L/48 gun. It fights enemy medium tanks well.

old text: The first version of the Pz.IV assault tank turned out to be ineffective against Soviet T34s and KVs. However, by the spring of 1942, the Wehrmacht started receiving new versions of the PzKpfw IV tanks, complete with upgraded armament and long-barrelled anti-tank Kwk40 guns, capable of defeating almost any opponent. In addition, the tank had good manoeuvrability, which -- along with its strong armor and powerful gun -- turned it into a fearsome combat vehicle.
new text: The Panzer IV Ausf. G has a long-barrelled Kwk40 anti-tank gun able to defeat almost any opponent. Good manoeuvrability and strong armor make it a fearsome combat vehicle.

old text: In order to clear minefields, German engineers developed a special mine roller. When mounted upon the chassis of a Pz.Kpfw.III tank, it allowed the vehicle to drive through minefields unharmed. The resulting corridors were then used by infantry and ordinary tanks. It was armed with only a machine-gun.
new text: This Pz.Kpfw.III carries a mine roller that lets it drive through minefields unharmed, clearing corridors for infantry and tanks. It is armed with only a machine gun.

old text: The PzKpfw III Ausf. F was intended to fight alongside other tanks, using the same 37mm PaK 36 type gun favoured by the infantry at that time. This cannon provided adequate armament until 1940. Thankfully, the Panzer III design accommodated a larger armament, greatly increasing its lifespan once a larger cannon was required.
new text: The PzKpfw III Ausf. F fights alongside other tanks with a 37mm PaK 36 type gun, adequate only until 1940. Its design has room for a larger gun.

old text: In the summer of 1944, the Wehrmacht received their heaviest tank destroyer ever -- the Jagdtiger. Built on the King Tiger chassis, its main drawback was its exceptional weight, which gave it low mobility. However, in terms of armor and firepower, this vehicle was unmatched -- its 128mm long-barrelled gun was able to destroy any adversary with ease, and the thickness of its armor maxed out at as much as 250mm.
new text: The Jagdtiger is the heaviest German tank destroyer, built on the King Tiger chassis with a long-barrelled 128mm gun and armor up to 250mm thick. Its exceptional weight makes it slow.

old text: Mounted on a wheeled carriage, the FlaK 38 gun was a further development of the FlaK-30 AA gun: lighter, but boasting higher rate of fire. It was used by the Wehrmacht and Luftwaffe for anti-aircraft defense. It could, however, be easily employed against infantry and lightly-armored vehicles.
new text: The FlaK 38 is a wheeled anti-aircraft gun, lighter and faster-firing than the FlaK-30. It can also be used against infantry and lightly-armored vehicles.

old text: The 88mm FlaK 18 was an anti-aircraft and anti-tank gun, mounted on a gun carriage that enabled it to fire in all directions. Widespread production started in 1933, and it soon proved to be the best anti-aircraft weapon available, when Germany intervened during the Spanish Civil War. It also turned out to be an excellent anti-tank weapon, as its high muzzle velocity and large calibre gave it the power and range to take out enemy armor. The success of this weapon lead to many variants, and it was one of the most recognizable German weapons throughout the war.
new text: The 88mm FlaK 18 is an all-round anti-aircraft gun whose high muzzle velocity and large calibre also make it an excellent long-range anti-tank gun.

old text: This heavy field howitzer design was based on the old 155mm French guns and entered into mass production in 1941. Intended for indirect fire on enemy personnel, fortifications and important shallow objectives, the M114 proved to be an excellent tool on the battlefield, and its easy maintenance, good ballistics and sturdy construction made it popular among US artillery troops.
new text: The M114 is a 155mm heavy field howitzer for indirect fire on personnel and fortifications. Easy maintenance, good ballistics and a sturdy build make it popular with US gunners.

old text: Before entering World War I, the United States was poorly equipped with heavy artillery. To address this problem a number of foreign heavy artillery guns were adopted, including the Canon de 155 mm GPF. After the end of the war development work began in the United States on a design to improve upon the existing models of heavy gun and carriage. A number of prototypes were produced in the 1920s and 1930s, but the projects were put on hold due to lack of funds. In 1938 the 155 mm Gun T4 on Carriage T2 was finally adopted as 155mm gun M1 on Carriage M1.
new text: The Long Tom, adopted in 1938 as the 155mm gun M1 on Carriage M1, is a US heavy gun developed to replace foreign designs such as the French 155 mm GPF.

old text: T48 57mm GMC - M3 based Gun Motor Carriage equipped with the M1 57mm gun, an American copy of the British QF 6 pounder anti-tank gun. A total of 962 T48s were produced during the war. Of these, 60 were supplied under lend lease to Britain, and 650 to the USSR - who called it SU-57 (99 rounds)
new text: The T48 57mm GMC is an M3-based gun motor carriage with the M1 57mm gun, an American copy of the British QF 6 pounder anti-tank gun. It carries 99 rounds.

old text: This anachronism of a self-propelled anti-aircraft gun was developed in 1945 and was primarily used for AA defense of vehicles on the move and in deployment sites. The M24 \"Chaffee\" chassis provided good speed and manoeuvrability, and two paired 40mm Bofors guns were able to engage not only planes, but also light and even medium enemy tanks. The first M19s were ready by the end of war, but never actually saw action. This is a World War II game you morons...
new text: The M19 is a self-propelled anti-aircraft gun with twin 40mm Bofors on the fast M24 Chaffee chassis. It can also hit light and even medium tanks, but is an anachronism from 1945.

old text: M4A1 76mm gun. Later M4A1 model received the larger T23 turret with a high-velocity 76mm M1 gun, which reduced the number of HE and smoke rounds carried and increased the number of anti-tank rounds. The first standard-production 76 mm gun Sherman was an M4A1, accepted in January 1944.
new text: The M4A1 76mm has the larger T23 turret with a high-velocity 76mm M1 gun, carrying more anti-tank rounds and fewer HE and smoke rounds.

old text: A Universal Carrier with a Ronson flamethrower fitted. This vehicle is a perfect asset when you have too much of the enemy existing in one place and you want to change that situation.
new text: The Wasp is a Universal Carrier fitted with a Ronson flamethrower, ideal when too many enemies gather in one place.

old text: A Universal Carrier with a Ronson flamethrower fitted. This vehicle is a perfect asset when you have too much of the enemy existing in one place and you want to change that situation.
new text: The Wasp is a Universal Carrier fitted with a Ronson flamethrower, ideal when too many enemies gather in one place.

old text: Mounted on a wheeled carriage, the FlaK 38 gun was a further development of the FlaK-30 AA gun: lighter, but boasting higher rate of fire. It was used by the Wehrmacht, Luftwaffe and SS troops for anti-aircraft defense. It could, however, be easily employed against infantry and lightly-armored vehicles.
new text: The FlaK 38 is a wheeled anti-aircraft gun, lighter and faster-firing than the FlaK-30. It can also be used against infantry and lightly-armored vehicles.

old text: The DShK 1938 is a Soviet heavy machine gun firing the 12.7x108mm cartridge. The weapon was also used as a heavy infantry machine gun, in which case it was frequently deployed with a two-wheeled mounting and a single-sheet armour-plate shield. It took its name from the weapons designers Vasily Degtyaryov, who designed the original weapon, and Georgi Shpagin, who improved the cartridge feed mechanism.
new text: The DShK 1938 is a Soviet 12.7x108mm heavy machine gun, often used by infantry on a two-wheeled mount with an armour-plate shield.

old text: Over a short period of time, three US companies -- Willys, Ford and Bantam -- worked together to develop a reliable and efficient off-roader to suit military needs. Production began in 1941, and it quickly proved its worth on the battlefield. Its excellent speed and its capacity to mount large-calibre machine guns made the Willys one of the finest army vehicles of WWII. This model is armed with a .30 cal M1919 A6 machine gun.
new text: The Willys is a fast, reliable US off-roader armed with a .30 cal M1919 A6 machine gun.

old text: Over a short period of time, three US companies -- Willys, Ford and Bantam -- worked together to develop a reliable and efficient off-roader to suit military needs. Production began in 1941, and it quickly proved its worth on the battlefield. Its excellent speed and its capacity to mount large-calibre machine guns made the Willys one of the finest army vehicles of WWII. This model is armed with a .50 cal M2HB machine gun.
new text: The Willys is a fast, reliable US off-roader armed with a .50 cal M2HB machine gun.

old text: Over a short period of time, three US companies -- Willys, Ford and Bantam -- worked together to develop a reliable and efficient off-roader to suit military needs. Production began in 1941, and it quickly proved its worth on the battlefield. Its excellent speed and its capacity to mount large-calibre machine guns made the Willys one of the finest army vehicles of WWII. This model is armed with a .50 cal M2HB machine gun and has armour plates installed to stop small-arms fire.
new text: The Willys is a fast, reliable US off-roader armed with a .50 cal M2HB machine gun, with armour plates fitted to stop small-arms fire.

old text: The M2 half-track was an armoured vehicle produced by the United States during World War II. M2 - White half-track with White 160AX engine. Fitted with a skate rail mount, featuring an M2HB machine gun. The first M2s were fielded in 1941, and would be used in the Philippines, North Africa, and Europe by the U.S. Army, and around the Pacific by the Marines.
new text: The M2 is a US armoured half-track with an M2HB machine gun on a skate rail mount.

old text: The M3A1 armoured half-truck was produced by the US from 1941 onwards, and used as a transport vehicle for tank corps and artillery divisions. Some vehicles were delivered to USSR as part of a lend-lease program. The spacious hull was made open-top. Along with a compartment designed to take eight soldiers, it housed a large-calibre machinegun, with mounts for additional machineguns on the rear and sides. The M3 proved to be a fast and reliable vehicle, well-suited for use in the harsh conditions of war.
new text: The M3A1 is a fast, reliable open-top US half-truck for eight soldiers, with a large-calibre machinegun and mounts for more machineguns on the rear and sides.

old text: In late 1940, US engineers undertook the project to adapt the 3-inch anti-aircraft gun T9 to an anti-tank role. The result was named the M5, and it entered service with the US Army in December 1942. Thanks to the high muzzle velocity of its round and its excellent armor penetration capabilities, this gun succeeded in replacing the early AT guns which were quickly becoming ineffective against new German tanks.

old text: The M1 mortar is an American 81 millimeter caliber mortar. It was based on the French Brandt mortar. The M1 mortar was used from World War II until the 1950s when it was replaced by the lighter and longer ranged M29 mortar.

old text: The Ordnance ML 4.2-inch mortar was a British. rifled 4.2-inch (110 mm) mortar used during the Second World War. It entered service in 1941. Use this mortar when you really want the enemy to cease fire.
new text: The Ordnance ML 4.2-inch is a British rifled 4.2-inch (110 mm) mortar, in service since 1941. Use it when you really want the enemy to cease fire.

new text: The M4 81mm MMC is an M2-based carrier with the 81mm M1 mortar, meant to be fired dismounted but able to fire to the rear from inside in an emergency.

old text: Mass-produced since April 1942, this self-propelled artillery gun was mainly used for infantry support. The 105mm field howitzer was mounted upon the chassis of a medium M3 tank, reinforcing the armament with a large-calibre AA machine gun. The impressive firepower of the main gun was supplemented by thick armor and excellent manoeuvrability for its class. The only shortcoming of the Priest was its open turret that left the crew vulnerable.
new text: The Priest is a 105mm self-propelled howitzer for infantry support on an M3 medium tank chassis, with a large-calibre AA machine gun. Thick armor protects it, but the open turret exposes the crew.

old text: The M2A1 was the standard field howitzer fielded by the United States. This field gun found wide use in both the Pacific and the European theatre. The gun was capable of firing its 105mm 20kg high-explosive ammunition at distances of 11 kilometres and more. The design was so successful that it was used well past the end of the war and some forms are still in use today.
new text: The M2A1 is the standard US 105mm field howitzer, firing 20kg high-explosive shells 11 kilometres and more.

old text: The 75 mm Gun Motor Carriage M3 was a United States tank destroyer and self-propelled artillery piece of World War II. It was the most numerous tank destroyer in United States Army service during the critical battles in North Africa and the Philippines; and continued to be used in more limited numbers in Sicily, before being declared obsolete in early 1944. The GMC M3 was then used by the regimental weapons companies of Marine regiments in 1944-1945 at Saipan, Peleliu and Okinawa.
new text: The 75 mm Gun Motor Carriage M3 is a US tank destroyer and self-propelled artillery piece. It is the most numerous US tank destroyer of North Africa, but obsolete by early 1944.

old text: The M3 was the logical advancement of the M2. The armour was increased, the chassis and the turret were modified from insights of armoured battles of 1939-40. In 1940 the M3 was accepted and entered production in 1941 at American Car & Foundry. While in production the turret was replaced with a more roundened version without riveted armour plates. Due to delivery problems, 500 M3 were supplied with the Guiberson T-1020 Diesel engines instead of the Standard Gasoline engine from Continental.

old text: The M4 Sherman, formally Medium Tank, M4, was the primary tank used by the United States in World War II. Thousands were also distributed to the Allies, including the British Commonwealth and the Soviet Union, via lend-lease. In the United Kingdom, the M4 was named after Union General William Tecumseh Sherman, following the British practice of naming their American-built tanks after famous American Civil War generals. Subsequently, the British name found its way into common use in the U.S.

old text: The M36 tank destroyer, formally 90 mm Gun Motor Carriage, M36, was an American tank destroyer used during World War II. The need for 90 mm gunned tank destroyers was so urgent that, during October-December 1944, 187 conversions of standard Medium Tank M4A3 hulls were produced by Grand Blanc Arsenal. These vehicles, designated M36B1, were rushed to the European Theater of Operations and used in combat alongside standard M36s. The M36 was well liked by its crews, being one of the few armored fighting vehicles available to US forces that could destroy heavy German tanks from a distance.
